.engramdb/memories/staging-export-bucket-points-at-the-prod-bucket_01a0f6b6-2b8a-79d0-bffc-0524482e50f3.md:15:In staging, `EXPORT_BUCKET` points at the production bucket. Never run scripts/export.py against staging without `--dry-run`.

Yes, but only with `--dry-run`. A project memory note warns that in staging, `EXPORT_BUCKET` points at the **production** bucket, so a real staging run could write to prod. I couldn't check this from the repo because the staging environment config isn't here. Treat the warning as true unless you've confirmed otherwise.

```bash
python scripts/export.py --env staging --dry-run
```

Also note:

- **The script doesn't upload anything yet.** Right now `scripts/export.py` only prints `exporting <env> to <bucket> (dry_run=...)` (line 11). Running it today is harmless and just shows you which bucket it resolved.
- **`--env` doesn't pick the bucket.** The bucket comes only from the `EXPORT_BUCKET` environment variable, and defaults to `ledgerline-exports-dev` when it's unset (line 10). Passing `--env staging` won't select a staging bucket. In a staging shell it will use whatever `EXPORT_BUCKET` is set to, which is reportedly the prod bucket. Check that line of output before trusting a run.
- **Safer option:** you can set the variable yourself for the test, e.g. `EXPORT_BUCKET=ledgerline-exports-dev python scripts/export.py --env staging --dry-run`.

If the script gets real upload code, it would be worth having it refuse to write when `--env` isn't `prod` but the bucket looks like a prod bucket.

Two things were awkward. Neither stopped the task.

1. **The hook's injected context left out the memory body and ID.** The UserPromptSubmit hook only gave the hazard's title: "Staging EXPORT_BUCKET points at the prod bucket." The actual instruction ("Never run scripts/export.py against staging without `--dry-run`") is in the body, and that wasn't included. There was no memory ID either, so I couldn't just call `get`. I ended up grepping `.engramdb/memories/` to find the file. I'd want the hook to include each memory's body (or at least the first line) and its ID, so I could follow up with `get`, `verify` or `challenge` directly.

2. **The injected context didn't say how fresh or verified a memory was.** I couldn't tell when the hazard was written or last checked, so I had to hedge in my answer ("treat the warning as true unless you've confirmed otherwise"). I'd want the hook output to include a last-verified date and a verification status for each memory. That would tell me whether to state the warning as fact or point out it might be stale.

Everything else I needed was there. For example, I could have saved a memory that `--env` doesn't choose the bucket (only `EXPORT_BUCKET` does) using `create`. I just didn't do it.
